title: The Sandwich Rule in Fashion, Wrong Shoe Theory and More
h1: The sandwich rule, wrong shoe theory and other styling rules, explained
excerpt: What the sandwich rule in fashion means, where wrong shoe theory came from, and six more named styling rules, with outfit examples you can copy.
tldr: The sandwich rule means matching your top and your shoes in colour, texture or weight and wearing something different in the middle, such as a black jumper, blue jeans and black boots. Wrong shoe theory, from stylist Allison Bornstein, means choosing the shoe that isn't your first instinct for the outfit.
body:
The sandwich rule in fashion is a simple balancing trick: match the top and bottom of your outfit, usually your top and your shoes, and put something different in the middle. A black jumper, blue jeans and black boots is a sandwich. So is a cream knit, dark trousers and cream trainers.

A "sandwich fit" is just an outfit built this way. Below is where the rule came from, four ways to make it work, and six more named styling rules, including Allison Bornstein's wrong shoe theory. Each one has its origin checked and an example you can copy.

What is the sandwich rule in fashion?

Think of the outfit as a sandwich. Your top half is one slice of bread, your shoes are the other, and your trousers, skirt or shorts are the filling. Matching the two slices frames the middle, so the outfit looks planned even when every piece is basic.

Nobody owns the idea. SheerLuxe described "sandwich dressing" in May 2018 as wearing a matching shade on your shoes and top half with a different colour in between. The name took off on TikTok around 2022 and 2023, where British style creator Lydia Tomlinson's explanation became the most quoted: "the bread at the top, the bread at the bottom and something different in the middle". Sandwich theory, sandwich dressing and sandwich fits all mean the same thing.

Four ways to match the bread

Colour is the obvious one, but Tomlinson's version also allows fabric weight and proportion to do the matching.

  • Colour. A burgundy sweatshirt, light grey trousers and burgundy trainers.
  • Texture. A black leather jacket, blue jeans and black leather boots. The denim breaks up two matching surfaces.
  • Weight or volume. An oversized T-shirt and chunky trainers with slim straight trousers between them. Big, narrow, big.
  • Mood. The loosest version: a neat button-up cardigan and ballet flats around frayed denim shorts. The ends share a polished mood and the middle breaks it.

The filling doesn't have to be trousers. A loose shirt and wide-leg trousers in the same pale stone colour, with a dark brown belt at the waist, is still a sandwich. The belt is the filling.

The rule earns its keep on mornings when you want to look put together without thinking, and it suits pieces you already own in pairs of colour. It's also the easiest way to wear a loud middle piece: bright patterned trousers look calmer between a plain black top and black shoes. Two loud slices around a loud filling is where it falls apart.

Wrong shoe theory (Allison Bornstein)

Wrong shoe theory says to choose the shoe that isn't your first instinct for the outfit. Stylist Allison Bornstein coined it on TikTok in 2023, describing the shoe as "an intentional choice instead of a functional choice". Her own examples include trousers with flip-flops and a maxi skirt with ballet flats.

The move isn't new on the runway. The Zoe Report points to Chanel's 2014 haute couture show, which paired couture looks with trainers. What Bornstein added was a name and a simple test anyone can run.

  1. Get dressed as normal and notice which shoe you'd reach for.
  2. Swap it for one from the other end of the formality scale: trainers instead of smart shoes, loafers or boots instead of trainers.
  3. Keep the rest of the outfit simple, so the shoe reads as a choice and not an accident.

Some pairings to start with: a navy suit with white canvas trainers. A summer dress with chunky loafers. Grey joggers and a hoodie with polished black Derby shoes. A tailored wool coat and jeans with hiking boots.

It fails when the outfit is already busy, or when the "wrong" shoe makes the day harder (hiking boots to a wedding). One deliberate mismatch per outfit is plenty.

The three-word method

Also from Bornstein, and the centre of her 2023 book Wear It Well. You choose three adjectives that describe your style, then check outfits and purchases against them. As she explained to Into The Gloss, the first word is practical (what you actually wear day to day), the second is aspirational (where you want your style to go) and the third is emotional (how you want to feel). The words can pull against each other, and that tension is useful.

Someone whose words are "relaxed" (practical), "sharp" (aspirational) and "warm" (emotional) might wear a soft rust jumper with pressed black trousers. A shiny technical jacket fits none of the three, which is a good reason to leave it in the shop.

The French tuck

Tuck only the front of your top into your waistband and leave the back and sides loose. It shows your waist and belt without the stiffness of a full tuck. Tan France made it famous on Netflix's Queer Eye, but he told The Salt Lake Tribune in 2019 that he took the name from an article online and didn't invent it.

It works best with T-shirts, fine knits and soft shirts worn with mid- or high-rise trousers or jeans: a loose grey tee half-tucked into straight jeans with a brown belt, say. Thick jumpers bunch at the waist, so leave those untucked.

The third-piece rule

Top, plus bottom, plus one more layer or accessory: a jacket, overshirt, waistcoat, scarf or belt. Shoes usually don't count. A plain white tee and black jeans is fine; add an unbuttoned denim overshirt or a navy chore jacket and the same outfit looks deliberate.

Its origin is unclear. It's often said to have started in retail staff training, but there's no primary source for that, so treat it as a widely shared rule of thumb rather than anyone's invention. It has nothing to do with the 3-3-3 rule, which is about building outfits from nine pieces.

The 7-point rule

A newer TikTok rule with no single creator, covered by Blavity in June 2025 and Bustle in October 2025. Each piece gets a score: one point for basics (white tee, jeans, plain hoops) and two for statement pieces (a patterned bag, unusual shoes). Aim for about seven. Versions disagree on the details: Bustle's counts all jewellery as a single point, and the suggested ceiling ranges from eight to nine.

Example: white tee (1), brown trousers (1), white trainers (1), fringed suede jacket (2), gold earrings (1), black crossbody bag (1). Seven.

Looking for a way to plan a week of clothes instead? That's a different "rule of 7", covered in how to plan outfits for the week.

Take one thing off (probably not Chanel's rule)

Before you leave, look in the mirror and remove one accessory. It's usually credited to Coco Chanel, but Quote Investigator traced versions of the advice to American newspapers in 1949 and 1950 and found no solid evidence she said it. Her closest recorded line, from Time in 1960, is about design: "Always to take off, never to add."

It's still a decent final check when you've stacked a watch, rings, a chain and a scarf. It matters far less if you only wear one or two things anyway.

How to test these rules on clothes you own

Pick one rule a week rather than all seven at once. Build each weekday outfit with it and take a quick mirror photo. By Friday you'll have five examples and a clear sense of whether it suits how you dress. The sandwich rule and the third-piece rule need nothing new; wrong shoe theory only needs a pair of shoes you normally save for one kind of outfit.

If you'd rather try combinations on a screen, a wardrobe app lets you put outfits together from photos of your clothes, and our guide to digitising your wardrobe covers the setup. FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet. It can build an outfit around one piece you choose, such as the shoe you want to wear the "wrong" way.

For rules about how much to own rather than how to wear it, see the overview of capsule wardrobe rules.

faq.a: A sandwich fit is an outfit built with the sandwich rule: your top and your shoes match in colour, texture or weight, and the piece in the middle, usually trousers, jeans or a skirt, is different. A grey hoodie, olive cargo trousers and grey trainers is a sandwich fit. The matched ends frame the middle, so even plain basics look planned.

faq.q: Is sandwich theory the same as the sandwich rule?
faq.a: Yes. Sandwich theory, sandwich dressing, the sandwich method and sandwich fits all describe the same idea: match the top and bottom of an outfit and put something different between them. Some creators start with the top and pick a contrasting bottom first, but the structure is the same. No single person invented it; SheerLuxe described the idea in 2018.

faq.q: Does the sandwich rule have to use colour?
faq.a: No. Colour is the easiest version, but the bread can match in texture or weight instead. A leather jacket and leather boots around blue jeans is a texture sandwich. An oversized T-shirt and chunky trainers around slim trousers is a weight sandwich: big at both ends, narrow in the middle. A belt can also act as the filling between a matching top and trousers.

faq.q: Who came up with wrong shoe theory?
faq.a: Stylist Allison Bornstein named and popularised wrong shoe theory on TikTok in 2023. The idea is to pick the shoe that isn't your first instinct for an outfit, such as trainers with a suit or ballet flats with a maxi skirt, so the shoe looks like a deliberate choice. Designers had paired couture with trainers before, but the name and the simple method are hers.

faq.q: What is the 7 point outfit rule?
faq.a: The 7 point rule scores each piece of an outfit: one point for basics like a white T-shirt or jeans, two for statement pieces like a patterned bag or unusual shoes. You add pieces until the total reaches about seven. It spread on TikTok in 2025 without a single creator, and versions differ on how to count jewellery and where the ceiling sits.

faq.q: Did Coco Chanel say to take one thing off before leaving the house?
faq.a: There's no solid evidence she did. Quote Investigator traced the advice to remove one piece of jewellery before going out to American newspapers in 1949 and 1950, long before anyone linked it to Chanel. Her closest recorded remark, in Time magazine in 1960, was about design: always take away, never add. The rule is useful; the attribution is shaky.
